newsitem.title: USA: Exclusive TV footage shows sickly Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Exclusive TV footage shows sickly Pol Pot.

text.p: Exclusive U.S. television footage on Monday night of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot showed a frail old man in ill health who appeared only mildly interested in a show trial by fellow guerrillas last week.
The television footage, excerpts of which were aired by ABC-TV's "World News Tonight," was obtained by Nate Thayer, an American journalist who witnessed the trial in northern Cambodia last Friday.

Pol Pot, dressed in a light green cotton shirt and dark pants, wore a black and white scarf during the trial and pulled it close around his neck as he was led away after being sentenced to house arrest for the rest of his life.
The dark eyes that flashed in the last television film of Pol Pot made 18 years ago -- just after the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" rule from 1975-79 -- now appeared dull and tired.
Pol Pot was the architect of that period, when more than a million Cambodians were killed by execution, torture, disease, starvation or hard labour.

ABC's Ted Koppel, who will air more of the footage on his "Nightline" programme later on Monday night, said Pol Pot suffered from malaria, high blood pressure and heart disease, and did not appear to have long to live.
Thayer, a correspondent with the Far Eastern Economic Review, told Koppel the guerrilla leaders had decided their verdict in advance of the trial after a lively internal debate.

"In fact, there was a debate within the leadership on whether to ... to kill him , cut him off from medical care, or give him the medical care that they could and allow him to live his final days under house arrest," Thayer said.

Thayer, the first foreign journalist to see Pol Pot in 18 years, said in a news release on Monday that the trial in front of some 500 Khmer Rouge cadres was clearly stage-managed but he said there was no doubt Pol Pot's downfall was genuine.
Hundreds of young men and women sat crowded in an open-air hut, listening intently as a succession of speakers denounced Pol Pot.

Khmer Rouge radio first denounced Pol Pot, now almost 70, in mid-June, shortly after a bloody split in the secretive Maoist group's top leadership in which defence chief Son Sen and almost a dozen members of his family were slaughtered.

Pol Pot and three of his commanders were found guilty of murdering Son Sen and his family, of "destroying national reconciliation" and of stealing money from the party, Thayer said. The three commanders were also said to have raped the wives of their comrades, he said.
Koppel said Pol Pot appeared ready to disappear again since he had been condemned to spending the rest of his life under house arrest.
